On 3/2/2004 at 10:47 PM ULLAS KARANTH <ukar...@vsnl.net> wrote:

From: ULLAS KARANTH <ukar...@vsnl.net>

Date: Tue, 02 Mar 2004 22:47:35 +0530
Subject:



> >Dear Len, Koustubh and List:
> >
> >I agree with most of what Len and Steve said on this issue,,, but..
> >
> >I am not sure Shorter Lines are always a good idea. It depends on what
> >species is being sampled. For ungulates and primates optimal survey times
> >in Indian forests are usually 06300-0830 hrs and again 1700-1900 hrs
> >broadly. Considering that you have to walk slowly trying to spot animals,
> >it makes sence to optimize the best available time by having the longest
> >transect lines that can be covered in this time interval of about 2 to 3
> >hours, which is usually about 3.5-4.0 km per line. If you make shorter
> >lines, you will not optimally use the time available for sampling (if you
> >consider the 'down time' of moving between lines).
> >
> >The other key issue is that for Distance estimation procedures to work,
> >the lines have to be placed with a random starting point. Unless these 9
> >lines are placed accordigly, there might be other problems, more important
> >than keeping the CV down.
> >
> >Hope this is of some use,
> >
> >Ullas Karanth
> >
>> >>*********** REPLY SEPARATOR ***********
>> >>
>> >>On 3/2/2004 at 9:38 AM Len Thomas wrote:
>> >>
>>> >>>Hi Koustubh, List,
>>> >>>
>>> >>>3 lines per stratum is far too few for reliable estimation of variation
> >in
>>> >>>encounter rate. Indeed 9 lines is rather too few even ignoring the
>>> >>>stratification. I think you should focus your survey effort on getting
>>> >>>more
>>> >>>(possibly shorter) lines. You will probably also have to reduce the
>>> >>>temporal
>>> >>>replication to achieve this.
>>> >>>
>>> >>>Section 7.2.1 of Introduction to Distance Sampling discusses transect
>>> >>>layout,
>>> >>>and warns against the dangers of overstratification. It may seem
>>> >>>intuitive to
>>> >>>stratify effort so that you put more effort per unit area into high
>> >>density
>>> >>>strata (see section 7.2.2.3), but if you end up with some strata with
> >very
>>> >>>few
>>> >>>lines in them you loose reliability. Since you are going to struggle to
>>> >>>have
>>> >>>enough lines per stratum for reliable estimation of encounter rate, and
>>> >>>you are
>>> >>>also going to struggle to have enough observations in your low density
>>> >>>stratum
>>> >>>to estimate detection function separately for that stratum, I suggest you
>>> >>>use
>>> >>>the same allocation of effort per unit area for all 3 strata (in other
>>> >>>words
>>> >>>same number of lines per unit area). That way you can combine the strata
>>> >>>together at the analysis stage if required, since coverage probability on
>>> >>>all 3
>>> >>>is the same (see section 7.2.1). This assumes you are mostly interested
>>> >>>in
>>> >>>estimating abundance in the forest as a whole. Alternatively you could
>>> >>>ignore
>>> >>>stratification altogether and allocate lines systematically throughout
> >the
>>> >>>study
>>> >>>area (rather than systematically within strata).
>>> >>>
>>> >>>If you could potentially have far more lines per stratum then look at the
>>> >>>allocation formulae of section 7.2.2.3.
>>> >>>
>>> >>>If you want to do stratified anlyses, but don't really have a good number
>>> >>>of
>>> >>>lines per stratum (but do have more than 3!), you could consider
>> >>estimating
>>> >>>spatial variation in encounter rate by estimating an overdispersion
> >factor
>>> >>>common to all strata -- see formula 3.127 and text around that, and
>> >>section
>>> >>>8.4.1 for a detailed example.
>>> >>>
>>> >>>With your current data, given the small number of lines I think you
> >should
>>> >>>regard the inferences you get as preliminary. If your 3 strata are equal
>>> >>>areas
>>> >>>then you have the same effort per stratum so you could try pooling strata
>>> >>>to get
>>> >>>more reliable inference (although the CV will be high due to high
>>> >>>variation in
>>> >>>encounter rate between lines). Alternatively, you could try the
>>> >>>overdispersion
>>> >>>method mentioned above. Since you have so few detections in the low
>>> >>>density
>>> >>>stratum you will have to estimate detection function pooled over strata
> >--
>>> >>>this
>>> >>>will cause some bias if coverage probability is not even across strata.
>>> >>>
>>> >>>Hope this helps,
>>> >>>
>>> >>> - Len
> >
